title: Shortest Job First: Why Order Changes Wait Time
topic: Shortest Job First scheduling — three jobs arrive together; running them in arrival order versus shortest-first changes the average turnaround time even though the total work is identical

beats.narration: Three jobs land at the scheduler at the same time. Same work — but the order you pick changes how long everyone waits.

elements.content: Three jobs, one queue — does order matter?

beats.narration: Job A needs ten units of CPU time, job B needs two, job C needs two. All three are ready at time zero.

elements.content: Three job tiles labelled A=10, B=2, C=2 lined up
the scheduler picks one — then the next — then the last

beats.narration: First-in first-out runs them in arrival order. A finishes at ten, B at twelve, C at fourteen. Average turnaround: twelve.

elements.content: Bar A grows from 0 to 10, then B 10..12, then C 12..14

beats.narration: Shortest job first runs the small ones up front. B finishes at two, C at four, A at fourteen. Average turnaround drops to six and two thirds.

elements.content: Same time axis, Gantt strip below
Bar B 0..2, C 2..4, A 4..14 — total work identical, distribution different

beats.narration: Same jobs, same total work — but the convoy of one big job behind two small ones is what hurts. Run short first, and everyone waits less.

elements.content: shortest job first nearly halves the average wait
(it needs to know job lengths up front — and that's the catch)
